text: Where other actors might be content to half-zombie-shuffle through low-budget films like this for an easy paycheck, Ridley’s commitment to her performance is admirable. We Bury the Dead has modest ambitions, and meets them for the most part.
If you turned it off five minutes before the credits roll, this would be a solid four-star movie.
It’s an interesting angle, and when it clicks, it delivers the occasional quiet sting. The problem is that it doesn’t quite bite down hard enough to be either genuinely moving or properly unnerving.
We Bury the Dead places the zombie outbreak as a backdrop instead of its main premise. This is more a film about grief and not letting go than a survival film.

A peculiar, singular and compelling take on the zombie genre that draws incredible tension from the lingering question: If not brains, what do the dead want from us? And what do they take from us, re-animated or not?

How gratifying it is to see such invention and fresh ideas wash through such a highly codified, convention-driven genre as the zombie movie...[it's] an excellent Australian take that adds new dimension to the well-worn zombie scenario.
An apocalyptic killscape is a roadmap to the suffering of the living.

While it never fully transcends its genre framework, it is thoughtful enough to feel like more than just another zombie movie – it is a meditation on grief dressed in the trappings of survival horror.
Grief as a subject for horror cinema has become a cliche, but We Bury the Dead at its best is getting at something more specific...

Might be the first zombie movie in which no living character is bitten by, and joins the ranks of, the undead; the movie itself, like its most unfortunate characters, is caught in an in-between state from which there’s no moving on
Ridley convinces throughout with a performance that essays both desperation and determination.
Daisy Ridley produces a masterclass in minimalism in this slick Australian zombie movie.
… there’s plenty to dig in We Bury the Dead.

...one of the most eerily realistic and relatable post-apocalyptic zombie movies in recent times. If you’re a fan of dystopian horror with a strong psychological thriller driver, where zombies are very much a part of the story as well, then...

At this point, the zombie genre is done to death. Or so I thought until I watched the Australian film We Bury the Dead. And it's a decent one, carefully avoiding the pitfalls of the genre tropes and being too sentimental.

Unlike typical zombie genre films, We Bury The Dead does not need to put the world at risk for us to care what happens, just Ava. Instead of breadth, it aims for depth — the stake is not human survival but one human’s survival.
Hilditch’s economical screenplay is far smarter than the average horror film that leans on special effects or a single clever concept to set itself apart.
We Bury the Dead is an extremely quiet, self-contained film, "small" in interesting ways, especially for this subgenre.

We Bury the Dead is a rumination on grief and the way we lose loved ones sometimes without a goodbye or on bad terms. It is also a road trip movie, a haunted house horror, and a showcase for the talents of Daisy Ridley.
... a thoughtful, restrained take on the zombie film genre.
